question: Move the AED at Edward A. Reynolds West Side High School into a 24/7 outdoor cabinet on the building's street wall.

evidence.text: Edward A. Reynolds West Side High School (School, ZIP 10029) has a registered AED at "11th Fl by cafeteria; FL 07; 9th Fl by Main Office".
Its hours come from: School building assumed open 7 AM to 6 PM on school days, September to June. Move the school-hours control to test other closing times.
Under that assumption it is reachable 55 of 168 hours in a school-year week, and 0 hours in a summer week if it is a school.
In 2025, an expected 1.18 cardiac-arrest 911 calls a year came from inside its two-minute walking area at hours when every AED in reach was shut (rank 10 of 100 NYC schools).
Within 400 m there are 10 other registered AED locations; 0 of them are open 24/7 by their published hours.
Citywide, a time-blind map puts 4.6% of call-weighted area within a two-minute walk of an AED; at the hour calls actually came in, 1.4% was within reach of one confirmed open.
Published research: a bystander shock with a public AED was associated with survival to discharge of 66.5% versus 43.0% without (Pollack et al., Circulation 2018, observed shockable public arrests).
Overture Maps lists ArchCare at Mother Cabrini Hospital, a hospital normally staffed around the clock, 292 m away: a possible alternative host for a 24/7 AED.
Unknown to this data: cabinet cost, vandalism risk, whether the school already allows after-hours access, and the actual location of each 2025 call inside the ZIP (only ZIP-level data is public).

turns.speaker: advocate
turns.text: Moving the AED to a 24/7 outdoor cabinet addresses a real gap in coverage. The school's current location is reachable only 55 of 168 hours weekly during the school year, and zero hours in summer [E3]. Last year, the area experienced 1.18 cardiac-arrest calls annually during times when every nearby AED was closed [E4]—ranking this school tenth among NYC schools for this problem. Research shows bystander shock with a public AED reaches 66.5% survival versus 43.0% without [E7]. While ArchCare at Mother Cabrini Hospital nearby offers an alternative [E8], a street-wall cabinet would ensure immediate access during the school's closed hours and summer months, directly serving the two-minute walking zone.

turns.speaker: skeptic
turns.text: The proposal rests on real data showing a coverage gap, but critical unknowns block a sound decision. Yes, the current AED is unreachable 113 hours weekly during school year and entirely during summer [E3], and 1.18 calls annually occurred when nearby AEDs were closed [E4]. However, we don't know the cabinet's cost, vandalism risk, or whether the school permits after-hours access—factors that could make this impractical [E9]. More importantly, Mother Cabrini Hospital 292 meters away is staffed around the clock [E8] and may already serve that zone faster than a street cabinet would. Before committing resources to outdoor infrastructure, the council should compare response times and costs against the hospital alternative and clarify implementation barriers.

turns.speaker: advocate
turns.text: The skeptic is right that Mother Cabrini Hospital sits nearby [E8], but proximity alone doesn't guarantee faster access. A hospital AED requires staff to retrieve and deploy it; a street-wall cabinet gives any bystander immediate access during the critical minutes before EMS arrives. The data shows this matters: citywide, only 1.4% of cardiac-arrest calls occur where an open AED is reachable [E6], yet bystander shock reaches 66.5% survival versus 43.0% without [E7]. The school's location ranks tenth among NYC schools for calls during closed-AED hours [E4]. A cabinet removes the retrieval step entirely and costs nothing to activate compared to relying on hospital staff availability. Unknown costs and vandalism risk deserve study [E9], but they are implementation questions, not reasons to accept preventable deaths when a proven intervention exists.

turns.speaker: skeptic
turns.text: The advocate makes a fair point that a hospital AED requires staff retrieval, but that doesn't settle whether a street cabinet is the best use of resources here. We don't know the cabinet's cost, maintenance burden, or actual vandalism risk in this neighborhood [E9]—factors that could be substantial. More fundamentally, the advocate hasn't shown that Mother Cabrini's response time would be slower than a bystander's retrieval of a street cabinet, especially since the hospital is staffed around the clock [E8]. The 1.18 annual calls during closed-AED hours [E4] is real, but without comparing actual response times and costs between a cabinet and the hospital alternative, we're guessing at which intervention saves more lives per dollar spent. Implementation barriers [E9] aren't minor details—they determine feasibility.

verdict.summary: Real coverage gap exists (1.18 annual calls during closed-AED hours, rank 10 of 100 schools), but critical unknowns—cabinet cost, vandalism risk, school access policies, and comparative response times versus nearby 24/7 hospital—block a sound decision.
verdict.strongestFor: School AED unreachable 113 weekly hours during school year, zero in summer [E3]. Bystander shock reaches 66.5% survival versus 43.0% without [E7].
verdict.strongestAgainst: Unknown cabinet cost, vandalism risk, school access policies [E9]. Mother Cabrini Hospital 292 m away staffed 24/7 [E8]—comparative response time unknown.
verdict.nextStep: Compare response times: street cabinet retrieval versus hospital staff deployment. Obtain cabinet cost, vandalism data for ZIP 10029, and school's after-hours access policy.
